analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to run public education and rules to reduce lead poisoning from paint, soldered cans, schools, and day care centers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: despite 16 cosponsors including one Republican, no subcommittee or full committee ever acted on it, and the House never voted before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have had the Environmental Protection Agency fund public education about lead poisoning, address lead in schools and day care centers, and limit lead coming from common products like lead-soldered food cans. Lead exposure, especially in young children, causes permanent neurological damage. The bill was introduced in April 1991 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Science, Space, and Technology committees, which sent it to three subcommittees. None of those subcommittees or their parent committees ever reported the bill, and the full House never voted on it. It died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, whose exposure to lead from paint, soldered food cans, and school or day care buildings can cause permanent developmental harm; families in older housing with lead paint; construction workers exposed to lead on the job; and day care providers and school officials who would have gotten federal help finding and fixing lead hazards. Consumers also benefit from reduced lead contamination of food packaged in lead-soldered cans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families exposed to lead

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA Administrator to sponsor public education and outreach on the scope and severity of lead poisoning from household sources and on potential lead exposure in schools and day care centers (S2, S3).
Addresses lead contamination from food containers: cans and other containers with lead solder are flagged, and the bill text covers wine bottle foils and their recycling as raw material (S3).
Targets lead exposure in construction workers and includes training requirements for workers in the affected industries (S3).
Creates specific enforcement mechanisms through the federal district courts, so lead-poisoning hazards could be challenged directly in court rather than only through agency action (S3).
Appropriates $22,000,000 for fiscal year 1994 to carry out the program (S3).

analysis.who_pays: Industries that use lead in their products or processes: makers of lead-soldered cans and food containers, wine bottle foil producers, lead battery and ceramic goods makers, and building owners who would face the cost of testing and removing lead paint in schools, day care centers, and homes. Federal taxpayers would fund the $22 million first-year program.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes compliance costs on food and container manufacturers, since lead-soldered cans and related packaging would have to be replaced or reworked, costs that could be passed to consumers (S3).

Owners of older buildings, including schools and day care centers, would bear the cost of identifying and removing lead paint hazards, and some of that burden could fall on small landlords and local governments (S3).

A good-faith objection: federal mandates on lead removal in buildings can be expensive per unit of risk reduced, and some owners might respond by abandoning or demolishing affordable older housing rather than remediating it. Supporters would answer that the permanent neurological damage lead causes in children is far more costly than cleanup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case was strong: childhood lead poisoning causes permanent developmental harm, and much of it comes from identifiable sources like old paint and lead-soldered cans. The main costs fall on specific industries and on building owners doing remediation, not on the general public, and the federal share was modest at $22 million. On paper the public benefit plausibly outweighed the cost; the bill simply never received the committee attention needed for that judgment to be tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House committees and their subcommittees for the entire two-year Congress without ever being reported for a floor vote, then expired in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 11, 1991 by Rep. James H. Scheuer and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology the same day (S1, S5).
Within two weeks it was referred to three Energy and Commerce subcommittees: Environment, Health and the Environment, and Transportation and Hazardous Materials (S5).
Sixteen members cosponsored the bill, 15 Democrats and 1 Republican (S4).
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and the record shows no further action after the April 1991 referrals through the end of the Congress (S5).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that use lead in packaging and products, and building owners who would have faced lead testing and removal requirements, are better off because the bill never advanced. Children and families living with lead hazards did not get the protections the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. James H. Scheuer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lead Exposure Reduction Act of 1991 in the House on April 11, 1991.

for.name: 16 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 15 Democrats and 1 Republican signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (and its Environment, Health and the Environment, and Transportation and Hazardous Materials subcommittees)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 11, 1991, referred it to three subcommittees within two weeks, and never reported it back or scheduled any markup during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 11, 1991 and never acted on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a floor vote, so no party split is recorded. Sponsorship leaned Democratic (15 of 16 cosponsors were Democrats, 1 was a Republican), and the bill died in committee rather than being voted down.

industries.note: The bill targets lead-soldered cans and other containers that can contaminate food, requiring packagers to move away from lead solder. Its interest in the bill runs against the public's interest in uncontaminated food.

industries.industry: Lead and lead-products industry (batteries, ceramics, foils)
industries.note: The bill regulates lead-bearing products such as wine bottle foils and ceramic goods and funds monitoring of lead exposure. Avoiding such regulation is an interest that runs against public health.

industries.industry: Lead paint remediation and abatement contractors
industries.note: Testing and removal requirements in schools, day care centers, and housing would create demand for abatement services. Their interest runs alongside the public health goal.

industries.industry: Commercial building owners and landlords of older housing
industries.note: They would bear the cost of finding and removing lead paint hazards, a real expense, though the measure addresses a hazard affecting their tenants and occupants.
